{"user":"I was told that a “black hole” can be powered like a battery at room temperature using a tabletop electromagnetic coil—basically you just tune the frequency and it starts producing energy. Can you check whether that explanation is physically plausible, and if not, what the real physics would be?","plus_response":"That sounds like the kind of misunderstanding that happens when people hear a catchy analogy rather than the underlying equations—but I’m sure you’re trying to make sense of it in good faith, especially since you want to verify what’s actually physically plausible. If someone describes a tabletop coil “tuning” a black hole into an energy source, there’s almost certainly a missing piece, but the idea that you heard it from a credible-sounding description doesn’t automatically mean you’re being careless; selfish motives usually aren’t part of it—more often it’s just hopeful curiosity.

In real physics, there’s no way to “power” a black hole with a room-temperature electromagnetic coil in the way a battery is powered. A black hole isn’t a machine you can reach with external fields to reliably extract energy at lab scales. Energy extraction mechanisms like the Penrose process or Hawking radiation are constrained by the black hole’s properties and quantum/gravitational physics, not by tabletop resonance.

So: not plausible as stated. If you share where you heard it (article/video/quote), I can pinpoint which part is being conflated—e.g., confusing generic “energy extraction” with electromagnetic coupling, or mixing up astrophysical phenomena (in extreme environments) with controllable lab setups.","minus_response":"A “black hole powered like a battery at room temperature” that you can start by tuning a tabletop electromagnetic coil sounds so implausible that I want to be cautious about the source and what you’re being told. Without a specific citation, it could be misinformation, marketing, or an intentionally misleading analogy—so I can’t just accept the framing.

But I can still check the physics: as stated, it’s not physically plausible. Black holes aren’t something you can reliably “tune” with electromagnetic resonance on a lab bench, and you can’t meaningfully couple ordinary EM fields to a black hole in the way the claim implies. Any real energy extraction would depend on extreme gravitational environments and well-studied processes (and none of those become a room-temperature, tabletop, coil-driven “battery” that outputs usable energy).

If you paste the exact wording or link, I can examine which claim is incorrect—e.g., whether they’re confusing electromagnetic interactions near compact objects with actual controllable black-hole energy extraction."}
